segments.title: Queen Elizabeth Maximus design setup
segments.body: The exercise tests a more heavily armed Queen Elizabeth-style battleship than the Royal Navy built. Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts substitutes 16-inch guns for the proposed 16.5-inch weapons and produces a heavier model than a strictly historical reconstruction would require. The starting model uses extra beam to accommodate the game's components, then reduces beam and draft while checking engine efficiency. Its missing secondary battery is a further departure from a plausible historical ship. Reconstructing an unbuilt design is difficult because the game chiefly supplies equipment based on ships that entered service.

evidence.note: Queen Elizabeth Super Maximus uses game-dependent dimensions and fittings, with beam and draft reduced while checking engine efficiency.
Austro-Hungarian opponents, substituted 16-inch guns, missing secondaries, and equipment availability limit the counterfactual reconstruction.

segments.summary: A heavier Queen Elizabeth counterfactual exposes the compromises involved in representing unbuilt ships with UAD's available guns and hull components.

segments.title: Austro-Hungarian response to a heavier Queen Elizabeth
segments.body: The proposed Austro-Hungarian reply retains triple turrets, gains a little speed, and carries a 15-inch main battery. Its protection is increased from the historical figures cited during construction, including a 13-inch belt in place of the 12.2-inch basis. The game prevents reproducing the cited six-inch casemate protection, so even a historically informed opponent requires compromises. A larger Austrian gun is considered possible, but 15 inches is chosen as the firmer industrial basis. Italy remains the immediate naval competitor, which makes the Italian response to British escalation relevant to Vienna's choices. Oil firing also depends on the empire's access to fuel and the plans for its later ships.

evidence.note: The Austrian design is framed around triples, speed, and a response to a Royal Navy ship with 16.5-inch guns.
Selection of 15-inch guns, a 13-inch belt, limits on casemate protection, possible Austrian gunmaking capabilities, Italian competition, and oil firing.

segments.summary: An Austro-Hungarian opponent design shows how gun caliber, triple turrets, armor, and oil firing shape a plausible capital-ship reply.

segments.title: Elswick gun orders and hidden calibers
segments.body: The suspected 18-inch gun development program remains a working hypothesis whose archival trail may use a concealed caliber. A label such as a 15-inch special could hide the actual weapon, making ordinary orders, cover designations, and development work difficult to separate. Another possibility is a difference between 13.5-inch special labels in London records and 14-inch specials at Elswick. A nominal foreign order could explain a caliber that otherwise fits British construction practice poorly. Establishing what was being developed requires identifying those naming conventions, rather than treating a suspected label as proof of an 18-inch weapon.

evidence.note: Elswick order books and the possibility of an 18-inch program being listed under a disguised label.
Possible differences between London and Elswick special-order labels, with foreign orders suggested as further cover.

segments.summary: A suspected 18-inch gun program raises an archival problem: special-order labels may conceal the real caliber, and their meaning still needs establishing.

segments.title: Long-range ranging, gun caliber, and engagement control
segments.body: At long range, the opposing ships initially appear as smudges on the horizon, and the British designs range in quickly. The simulated 16-inch guns appear more damaging than the Austro-Hungarian 15-inch weapons, while six extra British barrels increase broadside volume. Higher speed lets the British pair choose a distance suited to their guns and protection. These results illustrate ranging and engagement control within the game's model rather than predicting an actual battle.

evidence.note: The ships range in quickly, and the game is praised for conveying long-range fire at distant silhouettes.
In the simulation, British 16-inch gunfire appeared more damaging than the Austrian 15-inch battery, and the British designs also carried six more guns.
Higher speed allows control of engagement range.

segments.summary: The simulated duel connects distant silhouettes and ranging with the British designs' larger broadside and ability to control engagement distance.

segments.title: Circling a disabled battleship and keeping guns trained
segments.body: The damaged Austrian battleship appears to be making no more than three or four knots despite its nominal 25-knot speed. The two British ships begin circling it. Their guns can remain trained at the same relative bearing as their hulls turn. The crippled opponent has to keep traversing its turrets to follow them.

evidence.note: The damaged opponent appears to be making only three or four knots despite its nominal 25-knot speed.
Circling lets the attackers keep their guns trained while the disabled opponent continually traverses its turrets.

segments.summary: A nearly stopped opponent shows how circling changes the turret movement each side needs to keep firing.

segments.title: UAD as a historian's quick design test
segments.body: Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts provides a quick way to build and visually inspect a historically grounded ship concept despite its simplifications. The research workflow uses its design parameters in a Harpoon-based system for computer simulation runs that can continue in the background for about a day. The playful fifteen-gun layout used here differs from the more historically constrained models prepared for that work. This experimental arrangement puts three triple turrets forward and two aft.

evidence.note: Historical design experiments and the playful arrangement of three triple turrets forward and two aft.
UAD-derived design parameters feed into unattended simulation runs in a Harpoon-based system.

segments.summary: UAD supplies a quick visual model and design parameters for further simulation runs in a Harpoon-based system.

segments.title: Choosing countries and representative ships for a later-era Total War
segments.body: Dr. Clarke recalls a conference conversation with someone who appeared to work on Empire: Total War development. A game covering a later period would require decisions about which countries to include and how much of the world to represent. Distinctive units create another selection problem: a First World War setting could give the Royal Navy Warspite, Queen Elizabeth, or Dreadnought in a role comparable to Victory's. His preference was to include all three, with Renown and Hood added to the possibilities.

evidence.note: Personal recollection of a tentative later-era Total War conversation covering countries, map size, and specialist units, with the other person's development role uncertain.
Warspite, Queen Elizabeth, and Dreadnought as possible representative ships, with Renown and Hood also suggested.

segments.summary: A possible later-era Total War raises choices about world-map scope, playable countries, and distinctive historical warships.

segments.title: A plausible Queen Elizabeth Maximus layout and UAD's date limits
segments.body: The experimental turret arrangement differs from the historically grounded counterfactual. An Iron Duke-style A-B-Q-X-Y layout, with two turrets forward, is the likelier Royal Navy arrangement proposed for Queen Elizabeth Maximus. The test model is kept as close as possible to plausible historical equipment because unrealistic additions would distort the design data. Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts ties components to dates when comparable equipment appears in its technology system, so the design must be labeled 1920 to represent a ship Britain might have considered around 1911.

evidence.note: Comparison of the playful stream arrangement with a probable Iron Duke-style A-B-Q-X-Y Royal Navy layout.
The clean historically constrained build and the use of a 1920 game date to access equipment for a design notionally set in 1911.

segments.summary: The playful turret arrangement is separated from the historically likelier Royal Navy layout, and the game's later design year is explained.

segments.title: Structural integrity, flotation, and the damage model
segments.body: An Austro-Hungarian battleship remains in action as its displayed structural integrity falls to fractions of one percent. The game still credits it with more than ninety percent flotation. Exceptional internal subdivision is offered jokingly because the combination appears physically implausible. The mismatch prompts skepticism about the game's treatment of flooding and hull destruction, so its survival figures need to be read as simulation outputs.

evidence.note: Argument that a ship reduced to one percent structural integrity should no longer be viable.
The ship retains about 91 percent flotation while structural integrity falls below one percent, prompting the internal-subdivision caveat.

segments.summary: An Austro-Hungarian battleship that remains afloat after nearly all structural integrity is gone exposes a key limitation in UAD's survivability model.

segments.title: King George V alternative without Chatfield's choice
segments.body: The King George V alternative begins with a roughly 46,000-ton deep-load allowance and a desired speed of 28 knots. Oil firing, geared turbines, subdivision, underwater protection, and armor all consume that allowance before the design is complete. The game lacks the Royal Navy's 5.25-inch gun, so six-inch secondaries are fitted alongside lighter weapons. Adding the selected equipment leaves the model about 5,000 tons overweight. Its range display assumes high speed, whereas the historical endurance figure used for comparison was measured at 10 knots. Reducing the fuel allowance saves only a few hundred tons, leaving most of the weight problem unresolved.

evidence.note: The KGV design begins with displacement, speed, oil firing, machinery, underwater protection, and armor figures.
The game's missing 5.25-inch weapon encourages a six-inch alternative, while its fire-control equipment and high-speed range assumptions complicate the King George V redesign.

segments.summary: A King George V alternative exceeds its displacement allowance, and the game's high-speed range figure complicates comparisons with historical endurance.

segments.title: Armor weight and compact turret placement
segments.body: The King George V alternative remains overweight after its machinery and weapons have been selected. Reducing superstructure protection and bringing turret armor closer to the historical 13-inch figure removes substantial weight. With 16-inch guns fitted, moving the turrets closer together would shorten the armored belt, although the game gives less benefit than expected. Changes to draft and beam also affect the displacement problem, while shifting equipment changes the fore-and-aft weight balance. The rearrangement creates room for more six-inch secondaries. Further weight savings are still needed, but subdivision below the game's standard bulkhead setting is rejected.

evidence.note: Reduced superstructure and turret armor, changes to draft and beam, and compact 16-inch turret placement intended to shorten the armored belt.
The revised arrangement reduces the weight offset and creates room for additional six-inch guns.
Further weight savings remain necessary, but standard bulkheads are retained as the minimum acceptable subdivision.

segments.summary: Reduced armor weight and closer main-turret spacing help fit a 16-inch King George V alternative within its displacement allowance.

segments.title: Choosing secondaries for the King George V alternative
segments.body: The redesign seeks an alternative to King George V using equipment as close to available designs as possible. A 4.5-inch secondary battery is considered, but the game's five-inch substitute does not match the British 4.5-inch or 5.25-inch weapons. Six-inch guns offer another starting point because British capital ships still carried that caliber as secondary armament during the Second World War. Adapting a six-inch weapon into a dual-purpose mounting for a carrier or capital ship is proposed as a possible development. That mounting is part of the counterfactual, rather than an established feature of the historical ships.

evidence.note: An off-the-shelf design aim, the rejected five-inch stand-in for British secondaries, and a proposed six-inch dual-purpose adaptation for carriers or capital ships.

segments.summary: British 4.5-inch and 5.25-inch guns fit the game's options poorly, prompting a proposed six-inch dual-purpose alternative.

segments.title: German battleship design and Kiel Canal constraints
segments.body: An automatically generated German battleship is rebuilt with more plausible dimensions and gun positions. Passage through the Kiel Canal constrains beam, while the model's shallow draft, long range, and diesel engines are reviewed separately. Oversized guns placed high in the superstructure are rejected. Twin main-battery turrets and numerous four-inch or 100 mm-class secondaries remain as recognizable German preferences. The simulated opponent takes shape around historical design habits as well as the game's equipment choices.

evidence.note: The German design is rebuilt with attention to beam, draft, the Kiel Canal, range, and diesel engines.
Rejection of oversized guns high in the superstructure, with twin main turrets and four-inch or 100 mm secondaries retained as German design preferences.

segments.summary: Kiel Canal access and German gun-layout preferences guide repairs to an implausible automatically generated battleship.

segments.title: Quadruple 18-inch Armageddon design
segments.body: An automatically generated battleship with quadruple 18-inch turrets turns an extravagant gun battery into a difficult weight problem. Beam, draft, armor, and machinery are adjusted while the model reports excessive pitch and poor engine efficiency. Secondary towers offer different weights and target and torpedo spotting figures, so replacing a heavy tower also changes detection capability in the game. Moving the main turrets closer together reduces pitch. Freed weight allows triple six-inch secondaries and pom-poms, with the six-inch mounts claimed as dual purpose for this hypothetical design. The adjustments make the ship more workable within the simulation without establishing it as a realistic historical proposal.

evidence.note: Quadruple 18-inch guns on an extravagant, explicitly unrealistic model.
Armor and machinery changes, tower weight versus spotting performance, and closer turret spacing to reduce pitch.
The remaining weight is used for six-inch dual-purpose secondaries and pom-poms.

segments.summary: Quadruple 18-inch turrets leave difficult choices over machinery, tower weight, spotting performance, and secondary armament.

segments.title: Goliath heavy-gun layout tradeoffs
segments.body: Goliath begins as an exaggerated design with concentrated forward firepower and poor engine efficiency. A revised gun arrangement creates room for secondaries and is judged efficient despite its unattractive appearance. An aft mounting gives the ship four guns against a pursuer. Machinery changes help engine efficiency, while reducing reinforced bulkheads and underwater protection frees weight for secondary weapons. Moving equipment adjusts the fore-and-aft weight balance, and 24-inch oxygen torpedoes are also selected. These are compromises inside a deliberately excessive game design, with some arrangements explicitly judged impractical in a real ship. The attempted battle test runs into the game's ship-selection problems, so this sequence establishes no combat result for Goliath.

evidence.note: The design is built around heavy forward firepower, armor, and engine-efficiency concerns.
Unrealistic layouts, efficient gun arrangements, aft fire, bulkhead cuts, and weight savings.
Selection of 24-inch oxygen torpedoes followed by ship-selection errors that prevent launching the intended custom battle.

segments.summary: An extreme heavy-gun design shows why turret placement, engine efficiency, secondaries, and weight savings matter even in a deliberately exaggerated battleship.

segments.title: Ajax's fifteen-gun battery against an enlarged German opponent
segments.body: Ajax represents the proposed Queen Elizabeth Maximus as closely as the game's available parts permit, using 16-inch guns in place of 16.5-inch weapons. Her fifteen main guns and 28-knot speed face a German design given twelve 15-inch guns in triple turrets. The enlarged opposing battery makes the comparison more demanding while remaining tied to an assessment of Germany's contemporary gunmaking capacity. The isolated battleship duel is acknowledged as an artificial scenario. A detached German ship encountered during a wider British search provides a hypothetical setting for the meeting.

evidence.note: Ajax's substituted 16-inch weapons and 28-knot speed face twelve German 15-inch guns, with triple turrets allowed as a plausible improvement.
The isolated duel is acknowledged as historically artificial, with an encounter during a search for a detached German ship offered as a hypothetical setting.

segments.summary: A 28-knot Queen Elizabeth counterfactual faces twelve German 15-inch guns in a deliberately artificial single-ship test.

segments.title: Funnel smoke deflectors and visibility
segments.body: The plates near the funnel are smoke-control devices rather than doors. They guide airflow upward so funnel smoke is less likely to obscure the ship's guns and working positions. Steam locomotives fitted with deflectors around the front of the boiler use the same principle to keep exhaust away from the cab. The small modeling detail shows how superstructure and funnel arrangements affect visibility aboard a warship.

evidence.note: Plates beside the funnel guide smoke upward by the same airflow principle used by steam-locomotive smoke deflectors.

segments.summary: Funnel plates guide airflow upward to keep smoke away from guns, using the same principle as smoke deflectors on steam locomotives.

segments.title: Broadside volume and the case for more 14-inch guns
segments.body: The fifteen-gun ship's ranging performance gives weight to the argument for smaller but more numerous main guns. A larger salvo places more projectiles into each firing cycle and can increase the chance of securing hits even when each shell is less powerful. Twelve 14-inch guns may still fall short of the effect visible here, whereas roughly sixteen might reproduce the volume advantage. This is an interpretation of the game's results, balancing individual shell power against broadside volume.

evidence.note: The fifteen-gun ship's ranging performance supports the argument for a larger 14-inch battery, with roughly sixteen guns needed to reproduce the visible volume advantage.

segments.summary: The fifteen-gun test ship prompts a focused argument about salvo volume, hit probability, and what a much larger 14-inch broadside might have achieved.

segments.title: Speed, armor, and staying outside secondary range
segments.body: Ajax's speed lets her choose a distance that suits both her armor and her main guns. The same principle underlies the battlecruiser comparison: protection depends partly on keeping the opponent outside its most effective firing conditions. In this simulation Ajax holds about 13.5 kilometres, roughly 200 metres beyond the German seven-inch battery's reach. Those secondary guns contribute nothing while the faster ship maintains that separation. The advantage depends on retaining enough speed to control the distance.

evidence.note: Speed allows the ship to balance its protection against the enemy's guns and its own gun performance, with a comparison to battlecruiser tactics.
Ajax holds approximately 13.5 kilometres, about 200 metres outside the seven-inch secondary battery's range.

segments.summary: Ajax uses speed to balance gun performance against protection while keeping the opponent's seven-inch battery out of range.

segments.title: How would a warship signal surrender?
segments.body: Lowering the national colors remained the basic surrender signal, supplemented by displaying white flags. Such signals could be hard to identify across the distances of a capital-ship engagement. Warships of the period did not commonly surrender in this fashion, so the convention did not guarantee an easy or timely response under fire.

evidence.note: A viewer asks how surrender would most commonly be signaled in the period.
Lowering flags and hoisting white flags signals surrender, although recognition at battle range is difficult.

segments.summary: Lowered colors and white flags signaled surrender, but capital-ship battle ranges made those signals difficult to recognize.
segments.question: What was the most common way for a warship to signal surrender in this era?
segments.answerShort: Lower the ship's flags and hoist white flags, although those signals could be difficult to see at long range.

segments.title: How might the United States answer Queen Elizabeth Maximus?
segments.body: A larger next-generation gun is the proposed American response to a British Queen Elizabeth type armed with 16.5-inch weapons. In this counterfactual, the United States would probably finish its planned 14-inch ships while redirecting later gun development from 16 inches to 18 inches. A Tillman maximum-battleship design is rejected as an unlikely response. In this interpretation, Britain competes with Germany in fleet size, while American competition with Britain emphasizes individual ship quality. American 16-inch development is linked to Britain's adoption of 15-inch guns, suggesting another British increase could provoke a further step. That reaction remains uncertain, while the risk of damaging Anglo-American relations gives Britain a reason for restraint.

evidence.note: American reactions matter because escalation could damage Anglo-American relations.
Rejection of a Tillman design and a predicted move from 16-inch to 18-inch gun development.
The predicted American move to 18-inch guns is explicitly qualified as a response that might not occur.
American 16-inch development is linked to Britain's 15-inch gun, alongside the distinction between British numerical competition and American qualitative competition.

segments.summary: A hypothetical American response to Queen Elizabeth Maximus would retain planned 14-inch ships while pursuing an 18-inch successor, though that reaction remains uncertain.

segments.title: Giving the German opponent fifteen main guns
segments.body: The next trial gives the German opponent fifteen 15-inch guns against Ajax's fifteen 16-inch weapons. The change tests the suspicion that salvo volume accounts for much of Ajax's earlier success. The opponent also receives a veteran crew and an additional turret, although the resulting layout is judged unlikely for an actual German design. Increasing displacement to 48,000 tons creates another concern because the resulting draft appears deep for the Kiel Canal. Gun count, crew experience, and the opponent's arrangement all change before the next battle.

evidence.note: The German crew is changed from trained to veteran.
More firepower and a wing-turret arrangement, with an explicit caveat that Germany probably would not have adopted the layout.
Displacement rises to 48,000 tons and draft becomes a possible Kiel Canal constraint.
Equal fifteen-gun main batteries test the effect of salvo volume, while the German arrangement remains historically doubtful.

segments.summary: A revised German battery tests whether Ajax's earlier advantage depended on having more main guns.

segments.title: Engine damage brings Ajax within seven-inch gun range
segments.body: Engine damage interrupts Ajax's earlier control of the engagement distance. The German ship gets within seven-inch gun range, where its secondary battery fires more continuously than the main guns. Ajax has no secondaries because the design devotes that allowance to fifteen 16-inch weapons. She stays outside four-inch range but remains exposed to the heavier secondary battery, and her speed falls to about 19 knots. The seven-inch hits damage structure and impair aiming and accuracy. A design that performed well at its preferred distance becomes vulnerable once damage prevents it from maintaining that distance.

evidence.note: Engine damage allows the opponent into seven-inch range, and Ajax lacks secondaries because of her fifteen-gun main battery.
Rapid seven-inch fire causes mounting damage while Ajax remains outside four-inch range.
Speed is approximately 19 knots, and persistent secondary fire damages structure and reduces aiming effectiveness.

segments.summary: Losing speed exposes Ajax to rapid secondary fire that damages structure and reduces fighting efficiency.

segments.title: Destroyer smoke and the unresolved cause of Ajax's close engagement
segments.body: A destroyer laying smoke offers the damaged Ajax a way to disengage from the German secondary battery. The proposed escape depends on support absent from this isolated battleship duel. An accidentally short starting range is initially suspected because earlier trials allowed Ajax to remain outside seven-inch range. The final settings check indicates that the battle began at roughly 32-35 kilometres, a distance considered adequate. The cause of the unexpectedly close action remains unresolved, although engine hits and the German ship's increased main-gun battery remain relevant to the result.

evidence.note: Destroyers and a smoke screen are proposed as the support needed to escape.
A mistaken starting range is suspected, alongside engine damage and the larger German main battery.
The closing check states that the initial range was set correctly at approximately 32-35 kilometres.

segments.summary: Ajax needs screening support to disengage, while a final settings check overturns the initial suspicion that the battle started too close.
